articles.title: WWII hospital shipwreck in Albania now hosts devil firefish, squid eggs and a rare monk seal 80 years after sinking
articles.summary: Europe News: More than eight decades after the Hospital Ship ‘Po’ sank in Albania’s Vlora Bay, its rusting remains have become part of a busy underwater ecosystem..
articles.body: More than eight decades after the Hospital Ship ‘Po’ sank in Albania’s Vlora Bay, its rusting remains have become part of a busy underwater ecosystem. A new study has found the 134.98-metre wreck covered by dense biological communities, with fish, sponges, sea squirts and other marine life using its hard surfaces. The sighting was the first confirmed record in Vlora Bay since 1996. According to the research article published in Frontiers in Ocean Sustainability titled ‘First assessments on marine geomorphology and bio-colonization through the study and survey of the wreck of the Hospital Ship “Po” along the Albanian coasts (Vlora Bay)’ recorded the non-indigenous devil firefish and evidence of squid spawning around the wreck. Most strikingly, a critically endangered Mediterranean monk seal was photographed resting inside sheltered cavities of the ship in August 2023. Lying at depths of 33 to 37 metres within the Karaburun-Sazan Marine Protected Area, the wreck is now being studied not only as a remnant of wartime history but also as a structure that shapes local marine habitats and seabed conditions.Albania’s Hospital Ship ‘Po’ became a marine habitat in 1996The Hospital Ship ‘Po’ now supports a dense marine community in Vlora Bay, with more than 80% of its hard surface covered by biological growth. Researchers identified 54 taxa living on the wreck’s structure. Sponges, sea squirts, bryozoans, molluscs, algae and other organisms formed a layered community across the vessel. Fish surveys recorded 28 species from 14 families, including dusky groupers, morays, seabass, wrasses, seabreams and barracuda. Juvenile common two-banded seabream, painted comber and striped red mullet were also observed around the structure. The bow supported more complex assemblages than midship and stern areas.What did researchers find around the wreckAmong the most notable observations was the presence of the devil firefish, Pterois miles, a non-indigenous species recorded on the wreck’s hard surfaces. Researchers observed up to seven individuals at the same time. The survey also found large gelatinous egg clusters attributed to Ommastrephidae, likely Illex coindetii, attached to vertical surfaces at depths of 22 to 25 metres. These observations suggest the wreck may provide conditions suitable for reproduction and shelter. The study further recorded a transient Mediterranean monk seal, Monachus monachus, resting inside sheltered cavities in the upper structure.How does the wreck affect the seabed around itThe wreck does more than provide a surface for marine organisms. Its position also appears to influence the seabed around it. The 134.98-metre vessel lies upright at 33 to 37 metres depth and remains almost perpendicular to the dominant northwest-southeast water currents. Surveys identified a scour hollow reaching 2.1 metres below the reference seabed on the upstream side. Behind the stern, sediment formed a depositional trail extending about 45 metres. Sediment samples showed medium sand of about 350 micrometres at reference sites, while fine silt-clay particles below 63 micrometres occurred close to the wreck.Significance of the Hospital Ship ‘Po’ for future marine researchThe researchers describe the findings as an early step towards understanding how historic wrecks function within marine ecosystems. They developed two preliminary measures, the Geometric-Geomorphological Wreck Effect Index and the Ecological Hotspot Value Index, to summarise observations at the site. The ecological index was 0.83, based on benthic diversity, biological coverage and selected indicator groups.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday underscored the importance of the quality of teachers, who play a vital role in shaping the future of the country, a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday underscored the importance of the quality of teachers, who play a vital role in shaping the future of the country, and held National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE) can seek annual performance appraisal report (PAR) from teacher education institutions (TEIs).A bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said the role of NCTE in ensuring quality education for children is immense and teacher education has assumed greater importance since right to education has been recognised as a fundamental right under Right to Education Act.The bench stressed that it is necessary for the council and its bodies to ensure accountability of educational institutions. It quashed the HC order which had found fault with the council's decision to seek PAR from TEIs. "We fail to understand how a regulatory measure of a statutory body, empowered to achieve planned and coordinated development of teacher education system in the country, could be restrained from calling upon TEIs to file PAR. ...it is but natural and incidental that NCTE would require the stakeholders to provide the necessary PAR," it said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2009, Washington removed a century-old dike and let tides reclaim 762 acres; 21 miles of channels reopened, and young Chinook salmon entered the restored marsh in their first migration season
articles.summary: US News: Tidal water flowed back into the Nisqually River Delta for the first time in nearly a century after conservationists removed a large network of sea di.
articles.body: Tidal water flowed back into the Nisqually River Delta for the first time in nearly a century after conservationists removed a large network of sea dikes, quickly reopening miles of historic estuary habitat for threatened Pacific salmon. In autumn 2009, workers removed 4.5 miles of earthen dikes built in the early 1900s to turn the land into farmland. The work restored natural tidal flows across 762 acres of estuarine marsh at the Billy Frank Jr. Nisqually National Wildlife Refuge, making it the largest coastal wetland restoration project in the Pacific Northwest. Removing the barriers also reconnected 21 miles of historic tidal channels with Puget Sound. Within months, young Chinook salmon were found entering the newly flooded marshes during their spring migration towards the sea. The project was led by the US Fish and Wildlife Service in partnership with the Nisqually Indian Tribe and Ducks Unlimited. The goal was to help reverse long-term declines in Puget Sound Chinook salmon by restoring important nursery habitat where young fish could feed, grow and adjust to saltwater.Restoring the estuary engineFor more than 100 years, the Brown Farm Dike had blocked Puget Sound tides, turning rich coastal wetlands into enclosed freshwater farmland. While the change helped local agriculture, it badly damaged the natural function of the Nisqually Delta, which is the main transition area between the river's freshwater and the saltwater of Puget Sound. Removing the dike allowed saltwater to mix with freshwater from the Nisqually River again, quickly changing the landscape. High tides flooded mudflats that had been buried for decades, while water flowing back out created new branching channels across the muddy flats. Long-term studies by scientists from the US Geological Survey, NOAA Fisheries and the Nisqually Indian Tribe examined what happened after the dike was removed. According to research published in the Transactions of the American Fisheries Society, young Chinook salmon quickly moved into the new channels and used the restored marshes for feeding and growth. Monitoring by the NOAA Northwest Fisheries Science Center under Project ID 39213019 recorded a major increase in food available to young salmon, including estuarine amphipods and insects. The growing network of channels also gave young fish places to hide from predators while they adjusted to life in saltwater.Collaborative conservation across the watershedThe restoration was an important step in a decades-long effort by the Nisqually Indian Tribe and federal agencies to restore the entire Nisqually River watershed, from its source on Mount Rainier to Puget Sound. Before the 2009 project, more than 70 per cent of the delta's historic intertidal habitat had been lost to farming and land reclamation. Restoring tidal flows to the 762 acres brought back more than 80 per cent of the river's historic estuarine marshland. Project records from the US Fish and Wildlife Service also showed that restoring tides created important stopover habitat for migratory waterfowl travelling along the Pacific Flyway. Later surveys of estuaries around Puget Sound found that the Nisqually project created one of the largest additions of tidal channel length in the region in the previous three decades. The major changes created a more natural and varied habitat that could support larger numbers of young salmon than diked or channelised river mouths.A model for coastal resilienceThe recovery of the Nisqually River Delta has since become an important example for coastal restoration projects along the US West Coast. Scientists studying blue carbon have also used the site to examine how restored tidal marshes capture sediment and store carbon from the atmosphere over time. By replacing man-made barriers with natural water flows, the project showed that badly damaged estuaries can recover quickly when their connection to the tides is restored. Today, researchers continue to monitor the 21 miles of reopened channels. The data gives fisheries managers important information about how healthy estuaries can support the wider recovery of wild salmon populations in Puget Sound.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Moscow summons Norwegian envoy over seized ship in Arctic archipelago
articles.summary: Russia has summoned the Norwegian ambassador to the Foreign Ministry in Moscow after Norwegian authorities seized a Russian research vessel in a port in the...
articles.body:
Russia has summoned the Norwegian ambassador to protest the seizure of a Russian research vessel in the Svalbard archipelago by Norwegian authorities.

The vessel, Professor Molchanov, was detained in a port in Svalbard while en route from Murmansk to Barentsburg with staff, scientists, and supplies, due to Norwegian sanctions described by Moscow as a blockade.

The seizure was made at the request of Ukrainian state energy company Naftogaz, seeking to enforce a $4.2 billion compensation award against Russia for assets expropriated in Crimea, annexed by Russia in 2014.

Russia has summoned the Norwegian ambassador to the Foreign Ministry in Moscow after Norwegian authorities seized a Russian research vessel in a port in the Svalbard archipelago on Wednesday.

"The ambassador was conveyed a resolute protest against the actions of the Norwegian authorities, who had detained the Russian research vessel Professor Molchanov," the ministry said on Thursday.

The ship had been travelling from Murmansk to the Russian settlement of Barentsburg carrying staff from the mining company Arktikugol, scientists and food supplies.

The supply voyage to Svalbard - an Arctic archipelago belonging to Norway - had been made necessary by Norwegian sanctions that Moscow has described as a blockade. Russia is seeking the release of the vessel. Consular assistance is being provided to the crew and passengers, the ministry said.

The Professor Molchanov was seized by Norwegian authorities at the request of the Ukrainian state energy company Naftogaz, which is seeking to compel Moscow to meet outstanding financial obligations.

In 2023, an arbitration court awarded the Ukrainian state company around $4.2 billion in compensation for assets expropriated on the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.

articles.title: Two friends bought a 225-acre overgrazed Texas ranch that could support little beyond cattle; after restoring 100+ acres of prairie, planting 3,000 sand plums and adding a 5-acre wetland, wildlife returned
articles.summary: US News: When Jim Willis and John Webb bought a 225-acre ranch near the San Bernard River in Texas in 2000, the land had little wildlife left. Years of overgra.
articles.body: When Jim Willis and John Webb bought a 225-acre ranch near the San Bernard River in Texas in 2000, the land had little wildlife left. Years of overgrazing had left the property in poor condition, and the pasture could support little beyond cattle.According to Houstan Chronicle, the two friends, who were hunting partners, decided to change how the land was managed and bring back native plants and create better habitat for bobwhite quail and other wildlife.The ranch, known as WW Ranch, had been dominated by grasses that were commonly planted for cattle but did not provide the habitat needed by many native species. Willis and Webb began replacing these grasses with native varieties, including little bluestem and switchgrass.Their work eventually changed the ranch from a 'wildlife desert' into a place where quail and other grassland species could live. The restoration also connected wildlife habitat across neighbouring properties.Rebuilding the habitatThe first steps were not simple. Willis and Webb removed cattle from the property for a period so the existing non-native grass could grow. They then carried out a prescribed burn and applied herbicide. A second prescribed burn was later used to remove dead grass.In early winter, they planted native grasses and waited. Some of the grasses took more than a year to appear. Once the native vegetation had become established, cattle were brought back to the ranch.The cattle still had a role in managing the restored grassland. The small herd helped prevent the grasses from becoming too dense or too tall, while the animals' hooves also helped replant seeds.Willis and Webb also planted 3,000 native sand plum trees to provide woody cover for quail. They also added forbs, plants that produce seeds and attract insects. Insects are an important food source for quail hens and young chicks. The duo also enlarged a small, shallow pond to create a five-acre wetland area.According to the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, the work at WW Ranch included native prairie restoration on more than 100 acres, planting 3,000 native sand plum trees, creating a five-acre wetland and installing bird nesting boxes. The ranch also developed seven ponds and a pipeline distribution system for cattle and wildlife.Wildlife makes comebackThe changes were followed by the return of wildlife. Quail and 30 other species of grassland birds returned to the property, along with deer, ducks and migratory songbirds.The return of bobwhite quail was particularly important because the species is considered an indicator species. It means their population can reflect the condition of an ecosystem and the availability of suitable habitat for other grassland birds.Quail need grasses and plants that provide places for nesting as well as woody cover that can offer protection from predators, wind and heat.At WW Ranch, Willis said the property had developed a healthy population of about one quail per acre without any attempt to restock the birds.That success also convinced Willis that restoring one ranch alone would not be enough. He began approaching neighbouring landowners to create a much larger connected area of habitat.Restoration expandedWillis spent two years knocking on doors before another landowner agreed to transform their property. The idea gradually developed into a plan for a wildlife corridor linking neighbouring ranches with the Attwater Prairie Chicken National Wildlife Refuge.By 2008, 28 landowners had joined the project. Their properties ranged from 42 acres to nearly 8,000 acres. The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department and Audubon Texas were also supporting the effort with financial incentives and technical assistance. The goal was to create more than seven miles of connected, open habitat for grassland wildlife.Large working cattle ranches can provide space for native species, but dividing such land into smaller properties can make it harder for wildlife to survive."Habitat is the key," Kyle Brazil, a Texas Audubon biologist who worked with Willis, told the Houston Chronicle. "Where land is managed well for quail, it's managed well for all grassland birds."Convincing other landowners was not always easy. Some were concerned about the cost of temporarily removing cattle and carrying out prescribed burns.Willis explained that restoration could also provide practical benefits for ranchers. The Houston Chronicle reported that the work at his ranch cost about $100 per acre, with maintenance estimated at $5 per acre.Native grasses meant he did not need to buy fertiliser or hay, while the restored land could help with water and soil erosion. Willis said the land acted like a sponge when it rained and helped replenish aquifers. Income from cattle grazing and hunting leases could also help offset restoration costs.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
